informal_statement: For any function \( f \) that maps natural numbers to syntactic terms of a language \( L \), and for any judgment \( b \) in the lambda calculus \( (\Lambda \vdash \phi) \), the norm (i.e., a measure of complexity or size) of the term \( \text{rewrite}(f, b) \) is equal to the norm of \( b \).
informal_proof:
We prove this statement by induction on the structure of the judgment \( b \), generalizing over the function \( f \). 

1. **Base Case**:  
   For the simplest case, when \( b \) is a base term (such as a variable or a constant), applying \( \text{rewrite}(f, b) \) does not alter \( b \). Hence, the norm of \( \text{rewrite}(f, b) \) is the same as the norm of \( b \).

2. **Inductive Step**:  
   Assume that for all judgments of a certain complexity, the statement holds. For a more complex judgment \( b \), we again apply \( \text{rewrite}(f, b) \). By the definition of \( \text{rewrite} \) and the inductive hypothesis, each component of \( b \) maintains its norm after rewriting. Therefore, the overall norm of \( \text{rewrite}(f, b) \) remains equal to that of \( b \).

By induction, the statement holds for all possible judgments \( b \) and functions \( f \).

/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

This reflects the way in which the depth of a combination of two proofs is determined by the deeper of the two, plus an additional layer for the combination itself.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
